newsitem.title: HAITI: U.N. prepares for four more months in Haiti.
newsitem.headline: U.N. prepares for four more months in Haiti.

text.p: Haitians reacted with mixed feelings on Wednesday to a decision by the United Nations Security Council to extend the U.N. peacekeeping mission in the troubled Caribbean nation by four months.

While some residents welcomed the extension and the nation's police chief conceded that the neophyte Haitian National Police force was not ready to keep the peace, others say the peacekeeping contingent has begun to resemble an occupation force.

"On one hand, the troops don't bother anyone and maybe they stop someone with a plan to kill (President Rene) Preval," said a woman selling cigarettes and candy in the capital. "But it makes me feel like we can't manage our own affairs."
The U.N. Security Council, in a 15-0 vote, extended the mandate for a final four months, until the end of November, but trimmed its size.

The presence of the peacekeepers has become an increasingly controversial issue in Haiti. Grassroots political organisations staged a partially successful general strike on Monday, when demonstrators complained that the peacekeepers were an occupation force. Some Haitian political leaders also came out against the U.N. presence.
The Haitian National Police force, formed shortly after U.S. troops restored democracy in Haiti in the fall of 1994, was not yet experienced enough to maintain order, police chief Pierre Denize said.
"The security threat is still there and the police are still not ready," he said.

Enrique Ter Horst, the U.N. special representative in Haiti, said at a news conference on Wednesday the new mission would be called the United Nations Transition Mission in Haiti and that the reduced military component would leave after Nov. 30.
Ter Horst acknowledged the sentiment of some Haitians who are against what is increasingly being called an occupation, but noted the U.N. presence was at the request of Haiti's leaders.
The military force, comprised of Canadian and Pakistani soliders, will be reduced from 1,300 to 1000, with the United Nations funding only 50 of the peacekeeping troops.
The remainder will be funded voluntarily by the United States and Canada, according to U.N. spokeswoman Patricia Tome.
The U.N. peacekeeping mission followed the 1994 U.S intervention in which 20,000 U.S. troops restored to power former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide, who was ousted in a 1991 military coup.
